identification.summary: Storm-2372 is Microsoft's name for a device code phishing cluster active since August 2024 [S1]. Microsoft initially assessed with moderate confidence that it aligns with Russian interests, victimology and tradecraft, and described it as a suspected nation-state actor [S1]. A 31 July 2026 update on the Microsoft blog says Microsoft has further assessed Storm-2372 to be an initial access operations sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard, based on technical and operational overlaps [S1]. The actor poses as a prominent person relevant to the target on WhatsApp, Signal or Microsoft Teams, then sends invitations to online events or meetings that lead the victim to enter an actor-generated device code on the legitimate Microsoft sign-in page [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft uses 'Storm' for temporary, developing clusters; this one has now been folded into Midnight Blizzard as a sub-cluster per the July 2026 update [S1]. The update text was read through a fetch summary of the Microsoft page; confirm wording on the live page. Microsoft says it tracks other groups using similar techniques, including those documented by Volexity [S1]. Volexity separately reported several Russian actors (UTA0304, UTA0307, and CozyLarch assessed with medium confidence to overlap Midnight Blizzard/APT29) using device code phishing from about January 2025 [S2]. Do not merge Volexity clusters into Storm-2372 without a source stating the link.

attribution.sponsor: Russia (suspected). Microsoft: aligned with Russian interests; July 2026 update: sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard [S1]. No government attribution located.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft: moderate confidence in the original February 2025 assessment of Russian alignment [S1]. The 2026 sub-cluster assessment is stated without a confidence level in the text seen [S1].
attribution.basis: Microsoft cites Russian interests, victimology and tradecraft [S1] and, in 2026, technical and operational overlaps with broader Midnight Blizzard operations [S1]. Details of the overlaps are not given in the text seen.

objectives: Initial access to accounts at government, NGO and other organizations, followed by Graph API collection of email, including searches for credentials and government-related terms such as 'ministry' and 'gov' [S1]. Strategic intent is not stated by Microsoft beyond alignment with Russian interests [S1].

targeting.notes: Sectors and regions from Microsoft [S1]. Victim counts and named victims are not public in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: Social engineering of rapport via WhatsApp, Signal or Teams impersonating a relevant prominent person, then Teams-style meeting invitations where the device code is presented as the meeting ID [S1]. The actor generates legitimate device code requests, captures access and refresh tokens and so bypasses passwords [S1]. It then uses Microsoft Graph to search mailboxes for keywords (for example username, password, admin, teamviewer, anydesk, credentials, secret, ministry, gov) and exfiltrate email [S1]. It sends further device code phishing links from compromised internal accounts for lateral spread [S1]. By 14 February 2025 it used the Microsoft Authentication Broker client ID, obtained a refresh token, requested a device registration service token, registered an actor-controlled device in Entra ID, obtained a Primary Refresh Token and collected email from the connected device [S1]. It also began using proxies regionally matched to targets [S1]. Microsoft published no malware, domain, IP or hash indicators [S1].

campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed Storm-2372 activity since August 2024 against government, NGO and multi-sector targets in Europe, North America, Africa and the Middle East [S1].

campaigns.name: Microsoft public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Microsoft published Storm-2372 reporting, assessing moderate-confidence alignment with Russian interests and describing the WhatsApp/Signal/Teams lure and Graph API email theft [S1].

campaigns.summary: Microsoft updated its report: the actor switched to the Microsoft Authentication Broker client ID, registering devices in Entra ID to obtain a PRT, and began using regionally matched proxies [S1].

campaigns.name: Parallel Volexity reporting (separate clusters)
campaigns.summary: Volexity reported multiple Russian actors using device code phishing since about January 2025, including CozyLarch assessed with medium confidence to overlap Midnight Blizzard; this is separate reporting and not equated to Storm-2372 [S2].

campaigns.name: Reassessed as Midnight Blizzard sub-cluster
campaigns.summary: Microsoft updated its blog to say Storm-2372 is an initial access operations sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard [S1].

diamond.adversary: Suspected Russian state-aligned operators; initial access sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard per Microsoft's July 2026 update [S1].
diamond.capability: Device code phishing, impersonation lures on messaging apps, token and PRT theft via Authentication Broker client ID, Graph API mailbox search and exfiltration [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Regionally matched proxies are noted [S1]. No domains, IPs or hashes were published in the Microsoft text seen [S1].
diamond.victim: Government, NGO, IT, defense, telecom, health, higher education and energy organizations in Europe, North America, Africa and the Middle East [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Aligned with Russian state interests per Microsoft [S1]; specific collection requirements are not stated.
diamond.technology: Microsoft Entra ID / Microsoft 365 device code flow, Teams, Graph API, device registration service and PRTs; consumer messaging apps (WhatsApp, Signal) as the lure channel [S1].

gaps: No primary indicators (domains, IPs, hashes) were published in the Microsoft text read [S1].

The basis for the July 2026 Midnight Blizzard sub-cluster assessment (which overlaps) and its confidence level were not found; the update was read via a fetch summary, not verified on the live page [S1].
Volexity's original report could not be opened (host unreachable); its details come from secondary coverage [S2]. Relationship of UTA0304 and UTA0307 to Storm-2372 is not stated in sources gathered.
No government (CISA, FBI, NCSC) attribution or advisory was located.
Victim names, counts, and post-February 2025 campaign activity are not public in the sources gathered.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID was identified for Storm-2372; mapping to the Midnight Blizzard / APT29 record is unverified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the cloud identity plane (Entra ID, Microsoft 365 mail, Teams, Graph API) and personal messaging apps used by staff to reach contacts [S1]. STEP 2: The actor needs no malware or password; defender exposure is whether the device code flow is allowed and whether users can be rapport-baited [S1]. STEP 3: Template is impersonation on WhatsApp/Signal/Teams, then fake meeting invite with device code, token capture, Graph keyword search for credentials and government terms, internal re-phishing, then device registration and PRT theft [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued email collection against government, defense, NGO and telecom targets in allied regions. MDCOA is use of captured PRTs and credentials found in mail to pivot to privileged cloud accounts and maintain access after token revocation, which is plausible given the device registration step [S1]. Candidate indicators: device code sign-ins (error 50199 followed by success), new devices registered through the Device Registration Service shortly after, sign-ins from anonymized or target-region proxies, Graph mailbox access with keyword searches, and clicks on device login URLs [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: cloud identity telemetry (Entra sign-in logs, device registration events) must reach cyber defenders; no malware indicators exist to hunt [S1]. (2) Authorities: blocking device code flow and Conditional Access changes sit with tenant owners; confirm who may order them across mission partners [S1]. (3) Mission assurance: prefer phishing-resistant MFA and device enrollment restrictions; revoke refresh tokens when compromise is suspected [S1]. (4) Coordination: personnel contacted via personal messaging apps are outside enterprise monitoring, so reporting channels for suspicious outreach and sharing with coalition and DIB partners should be set up in advance [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: Storm-2372 is a suspected nation-state actor aligned with Russian interests, engaging in device code phishing campaigns targeting governments, NGOs, and various industries across Europe, North America, Africa, and the Middle East. The actor employs tactics that involve impersonating prominent individuals through third-party messaging services like WhatsApp and Signal to gain rapport before sending phishing invitations. These invitations lure users into completing device code authentication requests, granting Storm-2372 initial access to victim accounts and enabling Graph API data collection activities, including email harvesting. Microsoft has observed the actor utilizing keyword searches within compromised accounts to exfiltrate sensitive information.
